Conditional Collapse in Sign Language Production: A Diagnostic and a Coverage Argument Rui Hong Affiliation: George Mason University Jana Košecká Affiliation: {rhong5, kosecka}@gmu.edu Abstract The goal of Sign Language Production (SLP) is to translate natural language text into corresponding sign language movements performed by a virtual avatar. The quality of the
generated motion is typically evaluated by a motion-space Fréchet
distance (FID) and back-translation BLEU score on benchmarks
such as How2Sign [ 5 ] . The existing approaches can improve both metrics substantially while the
underlying generator fails to represent the input sentence
— a failure we call conditional collapse . In this work we
propose to evaluate the generated motion at three independent
levels: ( τ 1 \tau_{1} ) initial-pose conditioning, ( τ 2 \tau_{2} ) output diversity,
and ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) target faithfulness. We compute these as
pairwise-distance ratios using latent representations of a frozen
motion autoencoder (MoAE), judged against each dataset’s own
GT-vs-GT reference.
We evaluate diffusion and regression SLP models on How2Sign, including
a re-implemented Neural Sign Actors, and show that τ 3 \tau_{3} faithfulness is never attained, while FID varies by nearly two
orders of magnitude and is uncorrelated with faithfulness. We then
apply the same models and diagnostic to Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily,
and gloss-level ASL3DWord and show that faithfulness varies
proportionally to how densely the training sentences cover the test conditions
( conditioning coverage ) and not corpus size. The smaller but
densely covered Phoenix-2014T and ASL3DWord datasets generate faithful
sign motion, while CSL-Daily follows the input text yet falls short of
sign language faithfulness. Using the largest, open-domain How2Sign
dataset, the models collapse at every scale. We introduce two measurements of the text data
that rank the corpora in the order of how densely the training
sentences fill the embedding space, and how close each test
sentence lies to its nearest training sentence. 1 Introduction Sign Language Production (SLP) systems generate avatar sign language
motion from
text [ 19 , 1 , 24 , 26 , 29 ] and report steady benchmark gains. Reliable
evaluation requires metrics that respond to whether each output is
faithful to its specific input, not merely plausible under
the training distribution. We study this requirement in
sentence-level SLP, where systems on
How2Sign [ 5 ] report improving Fréchet
distance (FID) over motion features and back-translation (BT) BLEU.
We argue that both headline metrics can rise while the generator
remains essentially text-independent. FID rewards an
anatomically valid mean motion that ignores the input over a model
that follows the input but produces slightly noisier motion; it can
thus prefer a collapsed generator over a faithful one, as we observe
on How2Sign ( Sec. 5.2 ). On How2Sign, BT-BLEU is bounded by the BT
model. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not train a usable
translator, and the BT model collapses to high-frequency boilerplate,
reflecting token-frequency overlap rather than motion–text
correspondence. Beyond detecting this failure, we ask what drives it .
Our answer is a coverage argument: whether a generator learns to
condition on text is governed by conditioning coverage —
whether semantically close training sentences recur often enough in
the conditioning space for the text-to-motion correspondence to be
learnable. We show a corpus with 31 31 K paired sentences
collapsing while a 7 7 K-sentence corpus with denser coverage does
not. Contributions. (i) Given any text-to-motion model and a held-out test set, we
encode both ground-truth motions and model generations through a
frozen motion autoencoder MoAE (a small transformer) trained once on
the target dataset’s ground-truth motions, compressing each motion
into a compact latent vector and reconstructing it. We then compute
three pairwise-distance ratios in that space, varying the sentence
conditioning and comparing the generated and ground-truth motions;
faithfulness is judged against the dataset’s own measured GT-vs-GT
reference rather than a fixed threshold ( Sec. 3.1 ), and
a frame-level DTW check against a human–human alignability baseline
sharpens the verdict ( Sec. 6.2 ). (ii) We identify three indicators of conditional collapse
at different levels: an initial-pose level ( τ 1 \tau_{1} ), an output
diversity level ( τ 2 \tau_{2} ), and a faithfulness level ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) that can
be attained independently , with visual and quantitative
evidence ( Sec. 4 ). (iii) We run the same architectures, recipe, and diagnostic across four datasets spanning a
coverage spectrum: open-domain How2Sign, weather-domain
Phoenix-2014T [ 6 ] , daily-domain
CSL-Daily [ 27 ] , and isolated-gloss
ASL3DWord [ 4 ] , supported by measurements of the text data alone ( Sec. 6 ). Controls (text shuffling, frozen-encoder
swaps) rule out the text encoder; a retrained Progressive
Transformers [ 19 ] collapsing on
densely-covered Phoenix shows coverage is necessary but not
sufficient . The failures we document are diagnosable: report the diagnostic
ratios alongside FID and BT-BLEU, judge them against per-dataset
GT-vs-GT references, and be transparent about the coverage
properties of the training corpus. 2 Related Work Sign Language Production. Existing sentence-level SLP approaches fall into two families. Regression based models , such as Progressive Transformers (PT) [ 19 ] decode
poses autoregressively with a learned step counter; Huang et al. [10] decode non-autoregressively with a
graph-convolutional pose generator; T2S-GPT [ 26 ] generates dynamic-length VQ pose codes autoregressively.
A representative Diffusion-based model , MDM [ 21 ] , is a transformer denoiser
on frozen CLIP conditioning; G2P-DDM [ 24 ] runs
discrete diffusion in a VQ latent; Neural Sign Actors
(NSA) [ 1 ] is a GNN + + LSTM denoiser on SMPL-X
parameters. Hong and Kosecka [9] report usable MDM-style
generation at the gloss level on
ASL3DWord [ 4 ] (a WLASL [ 13 ] subset);
Signs as Tokens
(SOKE) [ 29 ] generates part-wise discrete sign tokens
with a pretrained language model across How2Sign, Phoenix-2014T,
and CSL-Daily, augmented by retrieving word-level signs from
external dictionaries — which we read as independent evidence for
the coverage account of Sec. 6 : word-level signs are
injected because sentence-level pairs alone do not cover the
conditions. We use SOKE’s released SMPL-X fittings as paired data
(its generator weights are unreleased). Sign Language Translation and BT evaluation. SLP approaches are commonly scored by back-translating generated motion
and reporting BLEU translation score. On How2Sign, no-pretraining translators plateau
near BLEU-4 1.2 1.2 [ 22 ] , reaching 8.03 8.03 with I3D
features [ 20 ] and ∼ \sim 12 12 only after 11 11 K-hour
pretraining [ 22 ] ; our own BT model plateaus at ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on GT motion. PT [ 19 ] and NSA [ 1 ] report scores of 10.51 10.51 and 13.12 13.12 without
pretraining, while independent retrainings place PT at 1.6 1.6 – 4.4 4.4 [ 10 , 24 , 26 ] and
note its dependence on GT timing. Evaluation critiques. FID’s limitations for conditional generation are known in
text-to-image [ 12 ] and
text-to-motion [ 7 ] domains, motivating paired R-precision
and multimodality metrics. Our diagnostic targets the conditional-mean collapse blindness dominant in SLP and
calibrates its verdicts against per-dataset GT-vs-GT references.
Pose-space DTW distances (DTW-MJE) are standard on
Phoenix-2014T [ 19 , 10 , 26 ] but are reported without a human–human baseline, which Sec. 6.2 supplies. Jiang et al. [11] meta-evaluate pose-based sign language
metrics by correlation with human judgment; we instead diagnose why generators fail. 3 Diagnostic Approach Let f θ f_{\theta} be any Sign Language Production (SLP) model, regression
or diffusion-based, that takes a sentence in natural language and
generates a sequence of human poses. Consider { ( t i , m i ) } i = 1 N \{(t_{i},m_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} the full test set, where t i t_{i} is the i i -th text input and m i ∈ ℝ T × D m_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D} its
ground-truth motion clip.
Let ϕ : ℝ T × D → ℝ d \phi:\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be a frozen
motion autoencoder MoAE, with latent dimension d = 256 d=256 .
We use T = 100 T=100 frames, per-frame D = 44 ​ upper-body joints × 3 = 132 D=44\text{ upper-body joints}\times 3=132 pelvis-relative 3 3 D coordinates, and train one MoAE per dataset on its train
motions only (see architecture in Appendix D). Define z i := ϕ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( t i , s 1 ) ) z_{i}:=\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1})) as the latent representation of SLP model
output, and z i ∗ := ϕ ⁡ ( m i ) z_{i}^{*}:=\phi(m_{i}) , the MoAE encoded GT motion for the
associated text sentence. We compute the following pairwise statistics: d inter \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{inter}} = 𝔼 i ≠ j ​ ‖ z i − z j ‖ 2 , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\,\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|_{2}, (1) d intra \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{intra}} = 𝔼 i ​ ‖ ϕ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( t i , s 1 ) ) − ϕ ⁡ ( f θ ​ ( t i , s 2 ) ) ‖ 2 . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\big\|\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1}))-\phi(f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{2}))\big\|_{2}. (2) Here s 1 ≠ s 2 s_{1}\neq s_{2} are two independent sampling seeds of a stochastic (diffusion)
generator; a deterministic (regression) model takes no seed, so f θ ​ ( t i , s 1 ) = f θ ​ ( t i , s 2 ) f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{1})=f_{\theta}(t_{i};s_{2}) . d inter ​ - ​ GT \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}} = 𝔼 i ≠ j ​ ‖ z i ∗ − z j ∗ ‖ 2 , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i\neq j}\,\|z_{i}^{*}-z_{j}^{*}\|_{2}, (3) d pair \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{pair}} = 𝔼 i ​ ‖ z i − z i ∗ ‖ 2 , \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\|z_{i}-z_{i}^{*}\|_{2}, (4) d pair ​ - ​ rand \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}} = 𝔼 i ​ ‖ z i − z π ⁡ ( i ) ∗ ‖ 2 . \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{i}\,\|z_{i}-z_{\pi(i)}^{*}\|_{2}. (5) Here π \pi randomly shuffles { 1 , … , N } \{1,\dots,N\} , leaving no index in
place, so z π ⁡ ( i ) ∗ z_{\pi(i)}^{*} is the GT motion of a different test
sample. Only d inter d_{\mathrm{inter}} and d pair d_{\mathrm{pair}} capture how the
output pose is affected by the input sentence and whether it lands
on the correct target; d intra d_{\mathrm{intra}} isolates pure
sampling noise, so input-driven variation can be told apart from it; d inter ​ - ​ GT d_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}} measures how much the GT motions of
different sentences naturally differ, so a small d inter d_{\mathrm{inter}} signals collapse only when it is small compared
to this natural spread; and d pair ​ - ​ rand d_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}} measures
whether the generated SLP output is closer to another example
other than its own GT. Three diagnostic ratios. From these statistics we form three unitless
quantities: a condition ratio (input-driven variance vs. sampling noise), a diversity ratio (output variance vs. GT
cross-sentence variance), and a faithfulness ratio (target
alignment vs. a random-GT baseline): ρ cond \displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{cond}} = d inter / d intra , \displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{inter}}/d_{\mathrm{intra}}, (6) ρ div \displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{div}} = d inter / d inter ​ - ​ GT , \displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{inter}}/d_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}GT}}, (7) ρ faith \displaystyle\rho_{\mathrm{faith}} = d pair / d pair ​ - ​ rand . \displaystyle=d_{\mathrm{pair}}/d_{\mathrm{pair\text{-}rand}}. (8) Since ρ cond \rho_{\mathrm{cond}} requires a stochastic sampling, a deterministic model has d intra = 0 d_{\mathrm{intra}}=0 (no seed dependence), making ρ cond \rho_{\mathrm{cond}} undefined. The other two ratios only need a single generation per
sentence, so they still apply; for deterministic models we report ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} and ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} only. FID measures a Fréchet distance
between two unconditional Gaussians fit to feature distributions: a
model whose outputs cluster around the GT marginal mean attains small
FID even when individual outputs f θ ​ ( t i ) f_{\theta}(t_{i}) are not faithful
motion representing their input t i t_{i} .
The guideline of ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} approaching 1.0 1.0 captures
this failure mode directly. The diagnostic requires no new training
(it reuses one frozen MoAE and O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) pairwise distances on
the full test split) and costs at most one extra forward pass per
sentence (the second seed for d intra d_{\mathrm{intra}} ; none for
deterministic models). 3.1 Per-dataset GT-vs-GT reference Table 1 : GT-vs-GT reference per dataset: same-text groups,
renditions, same-/different-text pair counts, and ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} ( Eq. 9 ); protocol and latent distances in
Appendix E. Dataset groups rend. same diff. ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} ASL3DWord (gloss) 100 339 874 113,708 0.752 Phoenix-2014T 50 325 4,399 6,500 0.874 CSL-Daily 1,000 2,731 2,504 54,620 0.673 How2Sign ( ≥ \geq 5 w., cross-video) 50 116 85 2,320 0.849 To interpret ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} we need a reference value. It is not zero.
Two genuine human renditions of the same sentence differ in
signer, speed, and style. For sentences that are signed by at least
two signers, we can measure ρ faith , ref = 𝔼 g , k ≠ k ′ ​ ‖ z g k ∗ − z g k ′ ∗ ‖ 𝔼 g ≠ g ′ , k , k ′ ​ ‖ z g k ∗ − z g k ′ ′ ∗ ‖ , \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{g,\,k\neq k^{\prime}}\|z^{*}_{g_{k}}-z^{*}_{g_{k^{\prime}}}\|}{\mathbb{E}_{g\neq g^{\prime},\,k,k^{\prime}}\|z^{*}_{g_{k}}-z^{*}_{g^{\prime}_{k^{\prime}}}\|}, (9) where g g indexes same-text groups and k k renditions within a
group: the numerator is the distance between two renditions of the
same sentence, the denominator the distance across different
sentences. It shows how close a second human rendition comes to the
target, measured from each dataset’s own ground truth. It is an
empirical reference, not a lower bound. A generator that outputs the
average of the valid renditions can fall below it without modeling
how signing varies. Because ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} differs across datasets, we propose no
absolute threshold for ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} . A model far above its dataset’s ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} has collapsed. Reaching the reference is consistent with
faithful generation but does not prove it. Table 1 lists the measured references and the
pairs behind them; CSL-Daily, built from scripted cross-signer
re-performances, is the strictest. How2Sign’s remaining exact repeats
are short greetings/fillers (“Hi!”, “Okay?”) whose clips carry no
sentence-specific motion and would push the reference to ≈ 1.0 \approx 1.0 , so we restrict to ≥ 5 \geq 5 -word cross-video repeats. 3.2 Stability of the diagnostic The numbers in Tab. 3 use the full test split of each
dataset, so the reported values do not depend on which subsample of
test sentences is drawn. Even on the full test split, almost every
sentence-level model evaluated on How2Sign attains ρ faith ≈ 1 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1 . A
fair concern is that this value reflects a problem with the metric
itself, not with the models: either (i) the MoAE cannot tell motions
apart in its latent space, or (ii) ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} always returns ≈ 1 \approx 1 regardless of input. We rule both out with two checks,
and add a third on what the MoAE resolves. (1) MoAE initialization. Re-training the MoAE from a
different random initialization (same architecture and data) and
re-running the diagnostic preserves the relative ordering of all
measured checkpoints; the diagnostic is robust to MoAE
training noise and not an artefact of one particular MoAE fit. (2) GT-vs-GT check: can ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} ever move? To rule out (ii), we feed the diagnostic the strongest possible
“alignment” case: a second GT rendition of the same sentence in
place of the model output. This yields the references of Sec. 3.1 ( 0.67 0.67 – 0.87 0.87 ), far below 1 1 , and the
healthy models of Sec. 6 reach them: the metric can
move; the collapsed models do not move it. (3) MoAE resolution on hands. Per-joint-group reconstruction
error (normalized RMSE, the fraction of motion not captured)
on full test splits: body/arms 0.17 0.17 – 0.20 0.20 , hands 0.30 0.30 – 0.37 0.37 — hands are harder but well encoded, so ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is sensitive to
the articulators carrying lexical content (facial expression is
outside the MoAE input; Sec. 8 ). 4 Three Levels of Conditional Collapse The ratios decompose SLP failure into three independent levels : τ 1 \tau_{1} Initial pose. Satisfied when the t = 0 t{=}0 pose varies
with the input text ( varied ); failed when every generated
initial pose is identical across sentences ( frozen ).
Visually inspectable in rendered output. τ 2 \tau_{2} Output diversity. Satisfied when outputs vary across
inputs as much as GT motions do; failed
when outputs cluster around a near-identical mean motion
( ρ div → 0 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}\to 0 ). τ 3 \tau_{3} Faithfulness. Satisfied when each output aligns to
its specific target and ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} approaches the dataset’s
GT-vs-GT reference ( Sec. 3.1 ); failed when alignment
is no better than random ( ρ faith ≈ 1 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1 ). These levels are independently attainable : a model can satisfy τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 2 \tau_{2} without attaining τ 3 \tau_{3} . On How2Sign, the checkpoints we
rendered show two visual cases. (i) Frozen start + + jitter trajectory (all three levels
collapsed): a near-identical canonical start regardless of input,
then small-amplitude noise around the GT marginal mean. This is the
dominant failure mode and includes the FID-best checkpoint (row 3 of Tab. 3 ). (ii) Varied start + + jitter trajectory ( τ 1 \tau_{1} , τ 2 \tau_{2} satisfied, τ 3 \tau_{3} collapsed): a visibly different start per input,
but the trajectory is still noise. It appears under aggressive
input narrowing (small vocabularies, short sentences).
The two full-corpus MDM checkpoints trained with the FK loss (rows 1
and 2 of Tab. 3 ) satisfy τ 2 \tau_{2} numerically. Their outputs
vary across inputs more than GT motions do ( ρ div ≈ 1.8 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}\approx 1.8 ), yet
each output is no closer to its own target than to a random one
( ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} 0.96 0.96 to 0.98 0.98 ). (iii) Varied start + + coherent motion (all satisfied) is
never observed on How2Sign; it is reached on the dense-coverage
datasets of Sec. 6 . Figure 1 shows the (i)-vs-(ii) contrast directly:
rows 1–2 emit a near-identical canonical start regardless of input
( τ 1 \tau_{1} collapsed), row 3 shows visibly different starts ( τ 1 \tau_{1} satisfied). Trajectory slices at five relative times
(Fig. S1) show small-amplitude input-independent motion
where the corresponding GT rows show coherent gestures — visual τ 3 \tau_{3} failure even for the strongest τ 1 \tau_{1} / τ 2 \tau_{2} checkpoints. Figure 1 : Initial generated pose ( t = 0 t=0 ) per checkpoint (rows);
each column is a different test sentence. Row 1: full How2Sign 26 26 K. Rows 2–3
( K = 3000 K{=}3000 , K = 500 K{=}500 ): training restricted to sentences within the
top- 3,000 3{,}000 / top- 500 500 vocabulary.
Rows 1 1 – 2 2 show frozen initial pose, identical regardless of the input sentence ( τ 1 \tau_{1} collapse); row 3 3 shows varied initial pose ( τ 1 \tau_{1} satisfied). Variant definitions
in Appendix A. 5 Experiments In all experiments, we refer to “checkpoint” as one fully
trained model with distinct design configurations (architecture, conditioning input,
dataset subset), trained from scratch and saved at the best epoch. Datasets. How2Sign [ 5 ] is an open-domain English
instructional ASL dataset: 31 31 K training / 2,357 2{,}357 test sentences with
per-frame SMPL-X [ 15 ] parameters; train
vocabulary 15,434 15{,}434 words.
Our default training pool keeps the ∼ \sim 26 26 K sentences of 3 3 – 30 30 words; a checkpoint trained on the unfiltered 31 31 K set
collapses identically (Table S1). Phoenix-2014T [ 6 ] is a dataset of German weather
broadcasts comprised of 7,092 7{,}092 train / 642 642 test sentences
and SMPL-X fittings from the
Signs-as-Tokens release [ 29 ] . CSL-Daily [ 27 ] is a Chinese daily-life
dataset comprised of 18,399 18{,}399 train / 1,176 1{,}176 test sentences with fittings,
from the same release [ 29 ] . Each training
sentence is performed by 2.8 2.8 signers on average, and test
sentences are unseen. ASL3DWord [ 4 ] is a dataset of isolated glosses with 1.2 1.2 K train / 339 339 test clips over 103 103 gloss types.
All four datasets use the same 53 53 -joint SMPL-X representation, so the
diagnostic pipeline
remains unchanged. Conditioning inputs. Next we vary the type of conditioning input and its representation. Sentence : the sentence is encoded into a single pooled
token by a frozen contrastive text encoder
CLIP-ViT-B/32 [ 17 ] for English and German, and
the Chinese-CLIP text tower [ 25 ] for Chinese ( Sec. 6.3 ). LLM keywords : we prompt an open-source instruction-tuned LLM
(Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [ 16 ] for English, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct for German and Chinese)
to reduce each sentence to a short list of representative content
words that will serve as a pseudo-gloss . This keeps the content
words (nouns, verbs, pronouns, negation, numerals, meaning-bearing
modals), drops function words, and lemmatizes the sentence.
The details can be found
in Appendix B.
A similar LLM extraction is used by Guo et al. [8] for sign
language translation. The keywords serve as the closest proxy gloss for How2Sign dataset that does not have gloss annotations; Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily provide native gloss annotations,
letting us compare LLM keywords against linguist-annotated gloss. Fused : sentence and keywords are concatenated into a single CLIP input (“ sentence ; keywords ”). Table 2 shows per language examples of gloss and LLM keywords. Additional examples can be found in Table S2. Note that LLM keywords keep source text order
while native gloss follows sign order.
All tested checkpoints vary only in the conditioning input . Table 2 : Example of keyword-extraction per language, with
the corpus’s native gloss where one exists. Keywords keep source
order; native gloss follows sign order (CSL-Daily topic-fronts the
location; DGS uses indexing signs such as IX ). Sentence Native gloss LLM keywords EN You don’t have to take big steps. — you not take big step DE teilweise kräftiger regen zieht heute nacht über uns ostwärts TEILWEISE REGEN KOMMEN IX teilweise kräftig regen ziehen heute nacht über uns ostwärts ZH 我要去超市买椅子，你去吗？ 超市 我 要 买 椅子 你 去 我 去 超市 买 椅子 你 去 Models. We evaluate two model families that together cover the recurring
design choices in SLP: iterative diffusion and single-pass regression. (i) Diffusion. Our main backbone is MDM [ 21 ] ,
a Transformer denoiser that receives the noisy motion sequence
together with a timestep token and the frozen CLIP text token, and is
trained to predict the noise (architecture in Fig. S2a).
It is trained with a per-frame pose MSE on the SMPL-X rotations plus a forward-kinematic
term ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} that penalizes 3 3 D joint-position
error after forward kinematics. One checkpoint (row 3 of Tab. 3 ) is trained with the pose MSE only; it attains the
best FID of all our How2Sign models and is included precisely because
FID ranks it first. (ii) Regression. As a deliberately simple non-diffusion
baseline we train a clean Transformer-decoder regressor: T T learned
frame queries pass through a 6 6 -layer decoder whose cross-attention
memory is the single frozen CLIP token, and the network emits the
full motion sequence in one forward pass ( ∼ \sim 26 26 M trainable
parameters; Fig. S2b). It uses the same pose and FK
losses as MDM. Because it is deterministic, ρ cond \rho_{\mathrm{cond}} is not defined for it.
For all models the architecture, text encoder, and training schedule
are held fixed across data and conditioning variants, so differences
between rows reflect the data or the conditioning input rather than
tuning; hyperparameters are listed in Appendix D. Evaluation. For each checkpoint we compute ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) and FID
on the full test split, render SMPL-X mesh videos, and visually
inspect initial pose and trajectory. 5.1 Main negative result We trained 14 14 sentence-level How2Sign dataset checkpoints
spanning two architecture families (diffusion, regression), two conditioning inputs (sentence, LLM keywords), while varying the four characteristics of the dataset: training-set
size ( 13 13 K/ 26 26 K/ 31 31 K), vocabulary restriction (top- 3,000 3{,}000 /
top- 500 500 training vocabulary), utterance length ( ≤ 3 \leq 3 words;
single word), and loss composition. Table 3 shows
representative checkpoints.
Every How2Sign checkpoint in Tab. 3 attains ρ faith ∈ [ 0.95 , 1.00 ] \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\in[0.95,1.00] , far above its GT-vs-GT reference of 0.849 0.849 , and no configuration attains τ 3 \tau_{3} . Holding everything
else fixed, growing the training pool from 13 13 K to 26 26 K
sentences (rows 4–5) worsens ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} ( 0.41 → 0.34 0.41\to 0.34 )
while ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays ≈ 0.95 \approx 0.95 , inside the collapse range.
Note that more data lets the model output the average motion more
confidently, yet it does not help the model to respond faithfully to
the input. Utterance length (Table S1). Decreasing T = 100 , 50 , 32 T=100,50,32 improves ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} monotonically ( 0.45 → 0.46 → 0.63 0.45\to 0.46\to 0.63 ) leading to shorter sentences satisfying τ 2 \tau_{2} . So τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 2 \tau_{2} can be satisfactory
by narrowing the input enough ( Fig. 1 : the

1–3; 0.731 0.731 matches ASL3DWord’s reference 0.752 0.752 . 5.2 The FID and ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} disconnect Across the 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints
and our NSA
re-implementation ( Sec. 7 ), FID spans from 1.91 1.91 to 151 151 while ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} spans only 0.89 0.89 – 1.00 1.00 .
The best-FID model (row 3) is the most collapsed
( ρ faith = 1.00 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=1.00 , ρ div = 0.17 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.17 ) and its outputs cluster tightly
around the marginal mean, which is exactly what FID rewards.
The Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily blocks agree: their lowest FID
( 1.39 1.39 , 1.34 1.34 ) is the regression row, also lowest in ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} .
Hence FID alone does not properly account for text-to-motion
alignment. The full table can be found in Table S1. 5.3 BT-BLEU also fails to track faithfulness We trained a motion-to-text back-translation (BT) model on How2Sign
without pretraining. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not
train a usable translation network. The video translator
of Uthus et al. [22] reaches only BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 in this
regime. Our BT model reaches BLEU-4 ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on
ground-truth motion, and 1.24 1.24 on our generated motion.
Its translation predictions are
often input-independent template language unrelated to the GT sentence
(see Tab. 4 ). The non-zero BLEU score is due to n-gram overlap with
high-frequency vocabulary where an autoregressive decoder in the back-translation model is estimating a
near-marginal prior. BT-BLEU on How2Sign therefore reflects the
weakness of the evaluator more than the quality of the generator. ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} captures this failure directly. BT-BLEU does not. Table 4 : Back-translation predictions for our generated motion on
the How2Sign test split (BLEU-4 = 1.24 =1.24 , no pretraining). They are
input-independent instructional template language or degenerate
repetition, unrelated to the ground truth. Evaluator details in Appendix C. Ground truth Back-translation prediction Boom, just like that. so, i’m going to take my right hand and i’m going to take my left
hand and i’m going to take my left hand to my left hand. Now it’s your responsibility to provide the healthy food. you can do it on both sides of the legs. Depending on the focus, if it’s a high-intensity workout … \ldots you can have a very, very light, and you can have a very light, very
light, very light, v … \ldots 6 The Coverage Argument In the following section we present a controlled experiment that sheds light on model collapse when training on How2Sign dataset and performance on the other datasets.
We use the same two architectures,
frozen text encoder, and diagnostic on four datasets that
differ in how densely their training sentences cover the conditions their test sets draw from. Each dataset uses its own MoAE and its
own GT-vs-GT reference. The diagnostic ratios are dimensionless and the values are compared across datasets only by band
membership , at-reference vs. far-above-reference values. 6.1 Same models, four datasets The main results on Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily, and ASL3DWord are reported in Tab. 3 .
On How2Sign, both architectures have a ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} gap of 0.10 0.10 – 0.13 0.13 above the 0.849 0.849 reference. On Phoenix-2014T both models reach ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} below the 0.874 0.874 reference. The generated motion is as close to
its target as another human rendition of the same sentence. All four conditioning-string variants stay in that
range ( Sec. 6.6 ); Fig. 3 a shows a
rendered generation against ground truth.
CSL-Daily’s reference ( 0.673 0.673 ) is the
strictest of the four, with training sentences performed by 2.8 2.8 signers on average.
Using the Chinese-CLIP text embedding [ 25 ] ( Sec. 6.3 ), all five
models attain ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} 0.75 0.75 – 0.80 0.80 ( Fig. 3 b).
On gloss-level ASL3DWord the same MDM backbone attains ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} of 0.731 0.731 against a 0.752 0.752 reference ( Fig. 2 ).
The largest corpus
(How2Sign, 31 31 K) is the one that fails its reference, while 4 × 4\times smaller Phoenix-2014T and 26 × 26\times smaller ASL3DWord approach
their reference. This corroborates the observation that more paired data does not produce faithfulness, and
less does not preclude it . It is the structure of the dataset that is the determining factor of the performance. Figure 2 : ASL3DWord test-set renders for two glosses ( black , hat ): GT on top, generation below, 5 5 frames per row
sampled at quantiles of GT cumulative motion energy (upper body).
The same MDM backbone that collapses on How2Sign produces the
target sign here (row 16 of Tab. 3 ). (a) Phoenix-2014T, recurring broadcast opener: 0.66 0.66 (human band 0.74 0.74 ) (b) CSL-Daily, unseen sentence: 0.70 0.70 (human band 0.59 0.59 ) Figure 3 : Best-aligned rendered test-set generation per dataset (GT
top, generation bottom) as DTW-matched frame pairs, with
DTW / / random per example ( Sec. 6.2 ). (a) “und nun
die wettervorhersage…” , inside the human–human band;
(b) an unseen CSL-Daily sentence (Chinese original in the
Appendix G), which reaches the generation p10 but not the
stricter CSL-Daily human band. Further examples in Fig. S3. 6.2 Frame-level alignment In Fig. 3 the generated frames visually track
their GT. To check whether this holds beyond selected examples, we
measure frame-level agreement directly, complementing the MoAE
ratios, which represent each motion as a single embedding vector.
We compare motions pose by pose with dynamic time warping (DTW):
we convert each motion into per-frame 3 3 D coordinates of the 44 44 upper-body joints, align the two sequences in time, and sum the
per-frame distances. This sum is divided by the same quantity
computed for pairs of unrelated sentences. We score two kinds of pairs. We take 40 40 sentences per dataset
that were performed at least twice and score the two human
renditions against each other: 0.74 0.74 on Phoenix-2014T and 0.59 0.59 on CSL-Daily. Note that the two renditions come from different
signers. For the models, we score the generated motion against the
GT of the same test sentence ( 40 40 sentences per dataset): 0.86 0.86 and 0.76 0.76 , farther from the GT than two humans are from each
other. Only the most repeated sentences close this gap
( Fig. 3 a). In short, passing the MoAE test does
not yet mean human-level frame-by-frame agreement: our “reaches
its reference” claims are about whole sequences (full protocol in
Appendix G). 6.3 Model-free evidence: dispersion and retrieval If the determining factor of collapse is conditional coverage, it should be measurable in
the conditioning space itself, with no generator involved. We test
this two ways. Table 5: Conditioning-space density (cosine similarity; higher = = denser): English CLIP for How2Sign and Phoenix; Chinese-CLIP for
CSL-Daily, since English CLIP barely separates Chinese sentences
(Appendix F). Mean-centered = = train centroid
subtracted, removing encoder anisotropy. Text-embedding cosine How2Sign Phoenix CSL-Daily zh {}_{\text{zh}} within-train pairwise 0.45 0.73 0.72 test → \to nearest-train 0.80 0.95 0.92 same, mean-centered 0.63 0.79 0.71 Conditioning space dispersion. On the frozen CLIP text encoder the generators condition on, we
measure (a) within-train dispersion : pairwise cosine among
training sentences, and (b) coverage : each test sentence’s
cosine to its nearest training neighbor ( Tab. 5 ).
Phoenix is far denser than How2Sign on every measure. Its 5 5 th-percentile coverage ( 0.89 0.89 ) exceeds How2Sign’s median ( 0.80 0.80 ); mean-centering preserves the gap ( 0.79 0.79 vs 0.63 0.63 ), and a natively multilingual XLM-R
encoder [ 3 ] preserves its direction, so the gap
is not an artifact of an English encoder reading German. CSL-Daily is measured on the Chinese-CLIP text
tower [ 25 ] ; its centered coverage ( 0.71 0.71 )
lands between How2Sign ( 0.63 0.63 ) and Phoenix ( 0.79 0.79 ), matching its
in-between model results. Nearest-neighbor retrieval sweep. For each test sentence, retrieve the nearest training sentence by
text embedding and use its GT motion as the prediction — an
architecture-free “model” whose faithfulness depends only on
coverage (full curves in Appendix F). On How2Sign, ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays flat at ∼ \sim 0.98 0.98 as the pool grows from 500 500 to 26,000 26{,}000 sentences
( 50 × 50\times ): even the nearest of 26 26 K training motions is, on
average, no closer to a test target than a random one. On Phoenix
the same sweep improves with pool size ( 0.905 → 0.867 0.905\to 0.867 ),
reaching the reference ( 0.874 0.874 ); on CSL-Daily (Chinese-CLIP) it
improves ( 0.888 → 0.868 0.888\to 0.868 ) but stays far above the 0.673 0.673 reference: test sentences are unseen, so no pool offers
a rendition to copy — and every CSL-Daily generator
lands below this 0.868 0.868 bound (rows 11–15 of Tab. 3 ), composing beyond retrieval. On How2Sign, more in-domain data adds no
coverage, so no model trained on it should be expected to condition
— and none does. 6.4 Text encoder effects Same encoder, opposite outcomes. The same frozen
English-pretrained CLIP text encoder reads German on Phoenix-2014T and the model is faithful ( ρ faith = 0.839 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.839 ) while encoding
English on How2Sign collapses ( ρ faith = 0.98 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.98 ). If weak text representations were the primary cause, this ordering would be reversed. Encoder swap. A more powerful frozen T5-base text encoder [ 18 ] in the 26 26 K How2Sign regression
leaves ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} essentially unchanged ( 0.954 0.954 with CLIP, 0.942 0.942 with T5). Text shuffling. On How2Sign’s unfiltered 31 31 K
sentence-MDM checkpoint (row 6 of Table S1), replacing
the input sentence moves the output 1.05 × 1.05\times , no more than re-sampling the
noise seed. Word-shuffling leaves
faithfulness almost unchanged ( 0.963 → 0.970 0.963\to 0.970 ), which suggests that the model
output is not affected by conditioning text. This is in contrast to Phoenix-2014T, where
sentence replacement moves the output well beyond
noise ( 1.35 × 1.35\times ) while word-shuffling moves it less than a new
seed ( 0.49 × 0.49\times ). ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays near the reference ( 0.838 → 0.855 0.838\to 0.855 ): the model reacts to the words themselves, not their order. 6.5 Coverage is necessary, not sufficient We retrained Progressive Transformers [ 19 ] ,
a representative of the autoregressive architecture family
on the same clean Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X data.
During inference (step counter
and output length governed by the model’s own predictions rather
than supplied from ground truth), it collapses ( ρ faith = 0.9999 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9999 ; output spread 0.025 × 0.025\times GT)
(see more details in Appendix H). To conclude: with sparse coverage every architecture we tested
collapses, and with dense coverage the architecture and training
protocol still decide the outcome. The diagnostic exposes both
kinds of failure. 6.6 Conditioning representation On the dense-coverage corpora we study the effect of the conditioning
representation, considering four options, sentence encoding,
LLM-extracted keywords ( Sec. 5 ), native gloss
(if available in the annotations), and a fused input. Native gloss
is the annotation upper bound for the LLM keywords: their gap on
annotated corpora measures the proxy’s quality where no annotation
exists (How2Sign). On How2Sign, using LLM keywords does not avoid
collapse (row 2 of Tab. 3 ). On Phoenix, all four alternatives stay at or near the 0.874 0.874 reference
(rows 6–9): once coverage is dense, no representation choice
re-introduces collapse. LLM keywords give the best faithfulness
( 0.809 0.809 ), matching or exceeding the linguist-annotated gloss
( 0.852 0.852 ). This is relevant for corpora like How2Sign that do not
have gloss annotations.
On CSL-Daily (Chinese-CLIP), all four cases share similar range
( 0.75 0.75 – 0.80 0.80 ; rows 11–15 of Tab. 3 ): LLM keywords ( 0.787 0.787 ) and
native gloss ( 0.788 0.788 ) are indistinguishable, so token order does not decide the outcome, and the fused
sentence ⊕ \oplus gloss input is best ( 0.750 0.750 ).
These differences are small (single runs); the
robust conclusion is that no conditioning text turns a collapsing
dataset into a healthy one, or the reverse. 7 Discussion Reproducibility note on Neural Sign Actors. NSA [ 1 ] reports the lowest sentence-level
How2Sign FID in the literature but releases neither code nor
weights. Following the published description, our re-implementation
needed several debugging rounds to converge; our best run reaches
FID ≈ 151 \approx 151 with ρ faith ≈ 1.00 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1.00 and no input-specific
motion in rendered samples. We do not interpret this discrepancy;
it does not affect our claim, since even an NSA-class FID is
consistent with τ 1 \tau_{1} / τ 2 \tau_{2} satisfied + + τ 3 \tau_{3} collapsed.
That is the best regime any of our How2Sign checkpoints reaches. We read prior FID
gains in this line as improvements in τ 1 \tau_{1} and partial τ 2 \tau_{2} ,
not τ 3 \tau_{3} . Reported successes on Phoenix and CSL-Daily. Qualitatively convincing generation is reported on
Phoenix-2014T [ 19 , 10 , 24 , 26 ] and CSL-Daily [ 29 , 28 ] ; that evidence
is structurally consistent with our frame-level analysis. The
displayed sentences concentrate on the densest conditions —
Progressive Transformers leads with the canonical broadcast opener,
three of SOKE’s four Phoenix examples are broadcast greetings —
precisely the conditions our DTW analysis places inside the human
band for our models as well ( Sec. 6.2 ). Every
figure shows one GT rendition and no human–human baseline, in formats that hide frame-level error, and
no verifiable generator weights were obtainable. Whether any attains
human-band frame alignment is thus open — and directly testable
with our released MoAE, references, and DTW protocol. This is not a
claim that these systems fail; it supplies the missing calibration. Recommended evaluation protocol. SLP papers should report ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) alongside FID
and BT-BLEU, judging ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} against the dataset’s GT-vs-GT
reference ( Eq. 9 ) on a shared released MoAE,
and, where same-sentence GT pairs exist, frame-level DTW
alignability against the human–human baseline
( Sec. 6.2 ). ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is a necessary-condition check: passing it does not certify linguistic adequacy, which
requires native-signer evaluation. What would fix How2Sign? Within-corpus scaling does not add coverage ( Sec. 6.3 ),
so the candidates are external: large-scale text-to-motion
pretraining, transfer from dense-coverage corpora, or word-level
supervision injected from outside the paired corpus — the route
SOKE’s dictionary retrieval takes [ 29 ] , consistent with
the coverage account. The sign-to-text direction points the same
way: a translator trained directly on How2Sign reaches only BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 , with faithful translation emerging only after 11 11 K
hours of pretraining [ 22 ] . None is evaluated under
our diagnostic here; pretraining remains plausible but undemonstrated. Societal impact. SLP evaluation rigor directly affects Deaf and hard-of-hearing
users: metrics that reward text-independent motion can promote
systems producing fluent-looking but meaningless signing. A
diagnostic calibrated against real signers’ renditions is a
prerequisite for trustworthy progress claims in accessibility. 8 Conclusion We introduced a training-free diagnostic that exposes conditional
collapse in sentence-level SLP, judged against per-dataset GT-vs-GT
references, and showed that (i) 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints across
two architecture families never attain faithfulness while FID
varies ∼ \sim 80 × 80\times uncorrelated with it, and (ii) the driver
is per-condition coverage: the same architectures reach their
sequence-level references on densely-covered Phoenix-2014T and
ASL3DWord with less paired data, condition partially on CSL-Daily,
and collapse on How2Sign at every available scale. A frame-level
DTW lens calibrated on human–human consistency is stricter still:
even at-reference Phoenix reaches the human band only on its densest
formulaic conditions. Coverage is necessary but not sufficient —
Progressive Transformers collapses on dense Phoenix — so the
diagnostic separates data-limited from architecture-limited
failure. We release the MoAE checkpoints and
diagnostic code under permissive licenses. Limitations. Our checkpoints do not cover the full design space; large-scale
text-to-motion pretraining remains untested. The MoAE
omits facial expression and non-manual markers, and hands are
reconstructed less precisely than body ( nRMSE \mathrm{nRMSE} 0.30 0.30 – 0.37 0.37 vs 0.17 0.17 – 0.20 0.20 ): ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} is a
necessary-condition check on manual articulation, not a certificate
of linguistic adequacy. Correlating the diagnostic with
native-signer judgment is the key next step. References [1] Vasileios Baltatzis, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias, Evangelos Ververas,

Input modality ( sent / keywords ). Sentence : the raw English How2Sign sentence, encoded by
frozen CLIP-ViT-B/32 [ 17 ] . LLM keywords : we prompt an open-source LLM to extract pseudo-glosses (short ordered lists of base-form content

unavailable for How2Sign, so the LLM keywords serve as the closest
available proxy. Training subset. The unfiltered How2Sign release has 31 31 K training sentences. Our default training pool is the ∼ \sim 26 26 K subset obtained by a 3 3 -to- 30 30 word sentence-length
filter that removes long-tail outliers; rows 1–5 and rows 8–14 of Tab. S1 use this 26 26 K pool. As an end-to-end check
that the filter is not load-bearing, we also trained an identical
MDM+sentence variant on the unfiltered 31 31 K-sentence release
(row 6): ρ faith = 0.98 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.98 matches the 26 26 K run exactly, and the
other diagnostic ratios fall in the same band. Beyond these two,
we evaluate a 13 13 K random subsample of the 26 26 K pool (row 7) and
two families of input-narrowing variants: vocabulary-restricted ( K=K ): sentences whose words
all fall within the top- K K most-frequent training vocabulary
( K=3000 , K=500 ); and short-sentence : short1 (single-word) or short3 ( ≤ 3 \leq 3 -word)
sentences drawn from the full 31 31 K-sentence release (these
bypass the 3 3 -to- 30 30 word filter by design). Exact train/test
counts are in Sec. D . Row labels combine the two axes
(e.g. K=500 keywords ). Each filter is applied to the raw
English sentence regardless of encoder input, so corresponding sent and keywords rows use identical training and
test sentences and differ only in what the encoder sees. Training and evaluation. Within each model family, the same training settings are used across
all data variants: batch size 256 256 , learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} ,
and 100 100 epochs for sentence-length variants; batch size 64 64 and 200 200 epochs for short-sentence variants. For each checkpoint we
compute ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) and FID on the full test split.
When training was vocabulary-restricted, we evaluate on the matching
test subset (the test sentences whose words also pass the filter). We
additionally render generated motions as SMPL-X mesh videos and
visually inspect them for τ 1 \tau_{1} and trajectory coherence. One axis at a time. Holding everything else fixed: quantity (rows 7 vs 8): 13 13 K → \to 26 26 K worsens ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} ( 0.41 → 0.34 0.41\to 0.34 ); ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays in the collapse band (both ≈ 0.95 \approx 0.95 ). More data lets the model output the average motion
more confidently; it does not teach the model to respond to the input. Vocabulary restriction (rows 8, 9, 10): shrinking the training
vocabulary from 15,434 15{,}434 to 3,000 3{,}000 and 500 500 types leaves ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} at 0.95 0.95 – 0.97 0.97 ; only the initial pose becomes varied at K = 500 K{=}500 (V+J). Utterance length (rows 10, 13, 14): T = 100 , 50 , 32 T=100,50,32 improves ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} monotonically
( 0.45 → 0.46 → 0.63 0.45\to 0.46\to 0.63 ); shorter sentences satisfy τ 2 \tau_{2} . Backbone (rows 1–4): the multi-scale MSTrans denoiser
( Sec. D ) changes FID by < 0.2 <0.2 and ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} by ≤ 0.02 \leq 0.02 .
So τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 2 \tau_{2} can be satisfied by narrowing the input
enough, but τ 3 \tau_{3} cannot: changing data quantity, vocabulary
density, sequence length, or backbone all leave ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} far above the 0.849 0.849 reference. FID range. Across rows 1–14 plus our Neural Sign Actors
re-implementation (Sec. 7; FID ≈ 151 \approx 151 , the upper
end), FID spans 1.91 1.91 to 151 151 while ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} spans only 0.89 0.89 to 1.00 1.00 ; the Pearson
correlation between them is near zero. Figure S1 : Trajectory slices at relative times t ∈ { 0 , T / 4 , T / 2 , 3 ​ T / 4 , T − 1 } t\in\{0,T/4,T/2,3T/4,T{-}1\} for the three checkpoints of

checkpoint lands right at it (renders in Fig. 2). This positive example is not a new
word-level SLP method; it confirms that the diagnostic tells working
models apart from collapsed ones. B LLM keyword extraction The LLM keywords conditioning input (Sec. 5) is
produced by prompting an open-source instruction-tuned LLM to reduce
each sentence to a short ordered list of base-form content words
(a pseudo-gloss). For English (How2Sign) we use
Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [ 16 ] with greedy decoding and max_new_tokens = 256 =256 ; for German (Phoenix-2014T) and
Chinese (CSL-Daily) we use Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with greedy decoding
and max_new_tokens = 96 =96 . No system message is used beyond
the prompt itself. Keywords are extracted once per sentence and cached;
every training variant of a corpus reads the same cache, so the
sentence, keyword, and fused variants of one corpus train on the
identical sample set (the length filter is always computed on the
original sentence). The prompts share one three-step recipe
(phrase-level chunking → \to keep/drop decision → \to citation form),
adapted per language: the German prompt handles auxiliary chains,
separable/particle verbs, and case inflection; the Chinese prompt
handles aspect particles, measure words, and the 把/被constructions, and requires
standard word segmentation. All three prompts instruct the model to
keep source order; the prompts are reproduced below with
instructions verbatim and the few-shot example lists abridged to
four per language. Table S2: Uncurated keyword-extraction examples in the three languages
(six random How2Sign training sentences; two sentences each for
Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily), with the corpus’s native gloss where one
exists. English: function words, copulas, and auxiliary chains are
dropped and the remaining tokens lemmatised. LLM keywords keep the
source sentence order, whereas native gloss follows sign order (the
CSL-Daily gloss topic-fronts the location
超市; the Phoenix DGS gloss uses
indexing and compound signs such as IX , WIE-AUSSEHEN that no text-only extractor can produce). The second German row shows
a lemmatization slip ( landeteil ); such artefacts are rare and
systematic, and do not change any verdict. languages next to the corpus’s native gloss where one exists. The
extractor is
imperfect: occasional artefacts include over-eager merging of adjacent
tokens and sporadic lemmatisation slips. These are systematic but rare
and do not change the conditioning regime: on How2Sign no keyword
variant escapes collapse, and on Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily the
keyword variants stay in the same band as the sentence and native-gloss
variants (Table 3). Fused input. The fused variant concatenates the sentence and its keywords
(Phoenix-2014T) or native gloss (CSL-Daily) into one string,
“ sentence ; keywords ”, which is then encoded by the same
frozen text encoder as a single pooled token. Nothing else changes. English prompt. The prompt below is sent to the LLM once per sentence, with {input_sentence} replaced by the source text and the
model’s output read as the keyword string. Arrows in the original
prompt files are rendered as -> here. You are an ASL (American Sign Language) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract pseudo-gloss from an English sentence. Pseudo-gloss is a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that an ASL signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’ Follow these three steps in order: ## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual words: - Auxiliary verb chains: ’’is going to’’, ’’has been doing’’, ’’would have been’’, ’’are going to be learning’’ -> mark the entire chain as auxiliary, drop it all - Phrasal verbs: ’’get out’’, ’’pick up’’, ’’break down’’, ’’set up’’, ’’hold down’’ -> mark as a single verb unit, keep the particle - Light verb constructions: ’’make sure’’->’’sure’’, ’’take a look’’->’’look’’, ’’get rid of’’->’’rid’’ — the light verb (make/take/get) is structural, drop it - Discourse frames: ’’let me/let’s’’ (when meaning ’’allow me to’’), ’’you know’’, ’’I mean’’ -> drop This step is critical: without it, ’’going’’ inside ’’is going to’’ would be mistakenly kept as ’’go’’. ## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in ASL: - Content words: nouns, verbs, adjectives, content adverbs (always, sometimes, often) - Pronouns: i, you, we, he, she, they, me, my, your, his, her, our, their - Negation: not, no, never, nothing, none, nobody - Interrogative WH-words: what, when, where, who, why, how, which (in questions) - Numbers: one, two, three, second, third, etc. - Modal verbs that carry meaning: can (ability), might/maybe (possibility), should/must (obligation) - Spatial/directional words when they express location or movement: inside, outside, up, down, around, forward, back, off, over Drop words that don’t change the core meaning: - Articles: a, an, the - Copulas: is, am, are, was, were (as linking verb) - Auxiliary chains identified in Step 1 - Conjunctions: and, but, or, so, because, if, that, then - Structural prepositions: of, to (infinitive marker), at, by, for, with, from (when purely grammatical) - Degree modifiers: very, really, pretty (as ’’fairly’’), quite, extremely, a lot — these are expressed through sign intensity in ASL, not as separate signs - Discourse fillers: okay, well, actually, basically, just, literally, essentially - Determiners: this, that, these, those, any, some (when not carrying meaning) - Relative pronouns: which/that introducing a clause (’’the button, which opens...’’ -> drop ’’which’’) - Structural ’’how’’: ’’learn how to play’’ -> drop ’’how’’ (vs interrogative ’’How do you play?’’ -> keep ’’how’’) If the same content repeats for emphasis in the original sentence, keep it only once (de-duplicate). ## Step 3: Restore to citation form Lemmatize each kept word to its base/dictionary form: - Verb tense: gives->give, went->go, tied->tie, learning->learn, spoken->speak - Plural: steps->step, hands->hand, feet->foot, children->child - Comparative/superlative: highest->high, bigger->big, better->good - Never produce a non-word fragment (e.g. other->oth is WRONG, keep ’’other’’) ## Output format Output ONLY the pseudo-gloss as a single line of space-separated lowercase words. No explanation. ## Examples Sentence: I’m having fun. Gloss: i fun Sentence: You don’t have to take big steps. Gloss: you not take big step Sentence: Hold down the second string on the fourth fret and then pluck the second and third string. Gloss: hold down second string fourth fret pluck second third string Sentence: Today we’re going to be learning how to play Portal, a game by Valve Software. Gloss: today we learn play portal game valve software [26 of 30 few-shot examples omitted for space] Sentence: {input_sentence} Gloss: German prompt. You are a DGS (German Sign Language / Deutsche Gebärdensprache) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract pseudo-gloss from a German sentence. Pseudo-gloss is a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that a DGS signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’ Follow these three steps in order: ## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual words: - Auxiliary chains: ’’ist gegangen’’, ’’hat gemacht’’, ’’wird kommen’’, ’’war gewesen’’, ’’sind worden’’ -> mark the entire chain as auxiliary, drop the auxiliary (sein/haben/werden), keep only the participle/infinitive lemma - Modal + infinitive: ’’kann gehen’’, ’’muss machen’’, ’’soll bleiben’’ -> keep the modal only if it carries meaning (kann=ability, muss=obligation), keep the main verb - Reflexive constructions: ’’sich freuen’’, ’’sich ärgern’’ -> drop ’’sich’’ (reflexive marker), keep the verb - Particle verbs: ’’aufstehen’’, ’’ankommen’’, ’’wegfahren’’ -> keep as one unit (already a single lemma) - Light verb constructions: ’’Bescheid geben’’->’’geben/inform’’, ’’in Verbindung treten’’->’’verbinden’’ — collapse to a single content word - Discourse frames: ’’und nun’’, ’’weiß ich nicht’’, ’’denke ich’’ -> drop the frame, keep the proposition ## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in DGS: - Content words: nouns (Wetter, Regen), verbs (gehen, regnen, sein-as-existence), adjectives (warm, kalt), content adverbs (heute, morgen, oft) - Pronouns: ich, du, er, sie, wir, ihr, mein, dein, sein, unser — DGS expresses these via IX (indexing) and POSS signs - Negations: nicht, nie, niemals, kein, keine, nichts, niemand, weder, ohne - Interrogative WH-words: was, wann, wo, wer, warum, wie, welcher - Numbers and quantifiers: ein/eine (when meaning ’’one’’, not as article), zwei, drei, viele, wenige, alle - Modal verbs that carry meaning: kann (ability), muss/soll (obligation), darf (permission), will (desire) - Spatial/directional words: oben, unten, hier, dort, vor, hinter, rechts, links — when expressing location - Time expressions: heute, morgen, gestern, jetzt, bald, früh, spät Drop words that don’t change the core meaning: - Articles: der, die, das, den, dem, des, ein, eine, einen, einer, eines (when used as articles, not numerals) - Copulas / structural sein: ist, sind, war, waren, sei, gewesen — when linking (’’ist warm’’ -> just ’’warm’’) - Auxiliary chains identified in Step 1: haben + Partizip, werden + Infinitiv (future) - Conjunctions: und, oder, aber, denn, weil, dass, obwohl, wenn, falls, sondern - Structural prepositions: in, auf, an, von, mit, für, bei, zu, nach (when grammatical/structural) - Degree modifiers: sehr, ziemlich, ganz, recht, durchaus — DGS expresses degree via sign intensity, not separate signs - Discourse fillers: also, eigentlich, halt, eben, mal, doch, ja, schon, nun - Vague quantifiers / particles: etwas, irgendwie, sozusagen - Impersonal ’’es’’: ’’es regnet’’ -> just ’’regnen’’; ’’es gibt’’ -> ’’geben/exist’’ - Filler relative pronouns: der/die/das as relative pronouns introducing subordinate clauses If the same content repeats for emphasis in the original sentence, keep it only once (de-duplicate). ## Step 3: Restore to citation form (German lemmatization) Lemmatize each kept word to its base/dictionary form: - Verb conjugation: gehe/gehst/geht/gingen->gehen; regnet/regnete->regnen; bin/bist/ist/war->sein - Plural: Tagen->Tag; Wolken->Wolke; Häuser->Haus; Männer->Mann - Adjective inflection: tiefer/tiefen/tieferes->tief; kräftige/kräftigen->kräftig; nächsten->nächst - Comparative/superlative: höher->hoch; größer->groß; am besten->gut - Decapitalize all words. DGS gloss is conventionally upper-case, but for our pipeline we output lowercase for tokenizer compatibility. ## Output format Output ONLY the pseudo-gloss as a single line of space-separated lowercase words. No explanation. No quotation marks. No leading punctuation. ## Examples Sentence: ich freue mich. Gloss: ich freuen Sentence: und nun die wettervorhersage für morgen donnerstag den zwölften august Gloss: wettervorhersage morgen donnerstag zwölft august Sentence: im nordwesten bleibt es heute nacht meist trocken sonst muss mit teilweise kräftigen schauern gerechnet werden Gloss: nordwesten bleiben heute nacht trocken muss kräftig schauer rechnen Sentence: was ist mit dem wetter morgen? Gloss: was wetter morgen [3 of 7 few-shot examples omitted for space] Now extract the pseudo-gloss for the following German sentence. Sentence: {input_sentence} Gloss: Chinese prompt. Note that the few-shot sentences of this prompt are deliberately not used as examples anywhere in the paper. You are a CSL (Chinese Sign Language / 中国手语) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract keywords (pseudo-gloss) from a Chinese sentence. Keywords are a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that a CSL signer would produce. The test is: ’’If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?’’ Keep the words in the ORIGINAL sentence order. Follow these three steps in order: ## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual characters: - Fixed expressions: 对不起, 没关系, 不客气, 谢谢, 再见 -> keep as ONE unit, do not split - Light verb constructions: ’’打手语’’->’’手语’’ (打 is structural), ’’叫什么名字’’->’’什么 名字’’ (叫 is structural), ’’取名字’’->keep the action verb 取 and 名字 - Aspect/structural particles attached to verbs: 了, 着, 过 -> drop the particle, keep the verb - ’’是……的’’ emphasis frame -> drop 是 and 的, keep the content inside - 把/被 constructions -> drop the marker 把/被, keep agent, patient, and verb ## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in CSL: - Content words: nouns (房间, 名字, 工作), verbs (去, 认识, 介绍, 起床), adjectives (好, 小, 高兴) - Pronouns: 我, 你, 他, 她, 我们, 你们, 他们, 这, 那 (when referring to a thing/place) - Negation: 不, 没, 没有, 别, 从不 - Question words: 什么, 谁, 哪, 哪里, 几, 多少, 为什么, 怎么 - Numbers: 一, 二, 三, 十, 五十, 100 — keep the numeral, DROP the measure word after it (个, 只, 条, 本, 张, 位, 岁 keep 岁 only when age is the point of the sentence) - Modal verbs that carry meaning: 会 (ability), 能/可以 (possibility/permission), 要/想 (desire), 应该/必须 (obligation) - Time words: 今天, 明天, 昨天, 今年, 现在, 每天, 早上, 晚上 - Location/direction words when they express real location: 上, 下, 里, 外, 前, 后, 旁边, 家 Drop words that don’t change the core meaning: - Structural particles: 的, 地, 得 - Aspect/sentence-final particles: 了, 着, 过, 吗, 呢, 吧, 啊, 呀 - Copula 是 when it just links (’’他是老师’’ -> 他 老师) - Existence verb 有 when a number already carries the meaning (’’我家有三个人’’ -> 我 家 三 人) - Measure words / classifiers: 个, 只, 条, 本, 张, 位, 件, 辆 - Conjunctions: 和, 跟, 或者, 但是, 因为, 所以, 如果, 虽然, 然后 - Structural prepositions: 在, 从, 到, 对, 给, 向, 跟 (when purely grammatical; keep when they express real location or destination) - Degree adverbs: 很, 非常, 太, 特别, 真, 挺 — CSL expresses degree through sign intensity, not separate signs - Discourse fillers and adverbs of emphasis: 就, 都, 也, 还, 又, 再, 其实, 当然 If the same content repeats for emphasis, keep it only once (de-duplicate). ## Step 3: Output as segmented words Chinese has no inflection, so no lemmatization is needed. Segment the kept content into standard Chinese words (not single characters unless the word is one character). Keep the original sentence order. ## Output format Output ONLY the keywords as a single line of space-separated Chinese words. No explanation. No quotation marks. No punctuation. ## Examples Sentence: 你叫什么名字？ Keywords: 你 什么 名字 Sentence: 我家有三个人。 Keywords: 我 家 三 人 Sentence: 你会打手语吗？ Keywords: 你 会 手语 Sentence: 这是我和我丈夫的房间，旁边那个小的房间是我女儿的。 Keywords: 这 我 丈夫 房间 旁边 小 房间 我 女儿 [12 of 16 few-shot examples omitted for space] Now extract the keywords for the following Chinese sentence. Sentence: {input_sentence} Keywords: C Back-translation evaluator: training details and failure modes Training setup. Our back-translation (motion-to-text) evaluator on How2Sign is
trained pose-to-text with translation cross-entropy only, no
gloss-CTC loss, no pretrained CSLR features, no auxiliary
pretraining. Input is axis-angle SMPL-X; decoding at evaluation is
beam- 5 5 ; the test split has n = 2,357 n=2{,}357 paired sentences. In
this regime BT-BLEU-4 plateaus at a ceiling of ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on
GT motion. Without pretraining, How2Sign alone does not train a usable
translation network, and cross-regime comparisons against
gloss-CTC-supervised evaluators (e.g. Sign Language
Transformers [ 2 ] ) are not directly meaningful. Failure-mode commentary. Table 4 shows 3 3 representative GT/prediction
pairs for our generated motion (BLEU-4 = 1.24 =1.24 ). The no-pretraining
video translator of Uthus et al. [22] reaches a similar
BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 . The pattern is consistent across the test
split: (i) input-independent high-frequency template language —
instructional constructions (“you can do it”, “you want to make
sure”, “i’m going to take my right/left hand”) and pronoun-heavy
filler — whose semantic content is unrelated to the GT motion; and
(ii) degenerate end-of-sequence repetition (“very light, very light,
very light, … \ldots ”). Both patterns are characteristic of an
autoregressive decoder estimating a near-marginal language-model prior
with negligible conditional signal from the encoded motion. A non-zero
BLEU score arises from short n-gram overlap with How2Sign’s
high-frequency vocabulary, not from recovered text content; the
diagnostic counterpart, ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} , captures this failure directly. D Implementation details MoAE. The MoAE ϕ \phi of the diagnostic is a small transformer autoencoder
operating on per-frame 3 3 -D joint coordinates: each SMPL-X axis-angle
sequence is first lifted to T × 144 × 3 T\times 144\times 3 joints by SMPL-X
forward kinematics, restricted to the 44 44 upper-body joints (spine,
head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, all 30 30 finger joints), and made
pelvis-relative, yielding per-frame input dimension D = 132 D=132 . A
linear projection lifts each frame to a d model = 256 d_{\mathrm{model}}=256 token; learnable absolute positional embeddings are added; a 3 3 -layer
transformer encoder ( 4 4 attention heads, feed-forward dim 512 512 ,
GELU, pre-LN) produces contextualized per-frame features. A masked
mean over valid frames (padding excluded) gives the 256 256 -dim
bottleneck z z . The decoder broadcasts z z across the target
sequence length, adds the same positional embeddings, runs through
another 3 3 -layer transformer stack with the same hyper-parameters,
and projects back to D D . Position embeddings are shared between
encoder and decoder; padding is handled with a boolean mask in both
directions. Training loss. For each batch we minimize per-frame MSE
between reconstruction and target plus an α vel = 0.5 \alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}=0.5 MSE on the first-difference (velocity)
of the reconstruction: ℒ MoAE = MSE ⁡ ( x ^ , x ) + α vel ​ MSE ​ ( Δ ​ x ^ , Δ ​ x ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MoAE}}\;=\;\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{x},x)\;+\;\alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}\,\mathrm{MSE}(\Delta\hat{x},\Delta x). The velocity term is essential: without it, the MoAE collapses to
emitting a per-sample mean pose at every frame, which would make z z insensitive to motion dynamics and defeat the diagnostic; the
encoder must retain information about how the body moves, not
only what poses it visits. Training: the target dataset’s
train motions only, sequence length T = 200 T=200 frames, batch size 128 128 , 100 100 epochs, AdamW [ 14 ] at lr 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , dropout 0.1 0.1 (eval at dropout 0 0 ), bf16 mixed
precision. The encoder is never exposed to model-generated motion
during training, so the bottleneck does not learn collapse-specific
features that could bias the diagnostic toward any particular
generator. The diagnostic has the limitations of any MoAE: a
poorly-trained MoAE could in principle push ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} artificially
close to 1 1 . We address this with a single frozen MoAE trained on the
target dataset’s GT train motions, the MoAE-initialization and
GT-vs-GT checks of Sec. 3.2, and an independent check
against visual classification of rendered outputs, which gives the
same conclusion on every checkpoint where we did it. One MoAE of this
architecture and recipe is trained per
dataset (How2Sign, Phoenix-2014T, CSL-Daily, ASL3DWord), and the same frozen checkpoint scores every diagnostic on that dataset,
removing per-paper feature inconsistency. A further MoAE of the same
architecture, trained on Phoenix-2014T MediaPipe keypoints
( 7,096 7{,}096 sequences), is used only for the PT experiment of Sec. H . Cross-dataset ratios are qualitative, not quantitative. The ratios ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} , ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} , ρ cond \rho_{\mathrm{cond}} are dimensionless within one ϕ \phi : numerator and denominator are L 2 distances in
the same latent space, so the random-pairing baseline cancels
the absolute scale. Therefore, within a single dataset, an ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} of 0.73 0.73 vs 0.96 0.96 means the model is genuinely more faithful, not
that one ϕ \phi was “stricter”. Across datasets, however, the latent
geometries differ and the same numerical ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} value need not
correspond to identical motion quality. We use cross-dataset
comparisons qualitatively only, to argue band membership
relative to each dataset’s own GT-vs-GT reference
( Sec. E ): ASL3DWord 0.73 0.73 against its reference of 0.752 0.752 ; Phoenix-2014T 0.81 0.81 – 0.85 0.85 against 0.874 0.874 ; CSL-Daily 0.75 0.75 – 0.80 0.80 against 0.673 0.673 ; How2Sign 0.89 0.89 – 1.00 1.00 against 0.849 0.849 — never as an ordinal ranking of two distinct-dataset
checkpoints by raw ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} . ASL3DWord MoAE calibration. The diffusion checkpoint’s ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 on gloss-level ASL3DWord
(row 16 of Tab. S1 ) is interpreted against the
within-ASL3DWord GT-vs-GT reference: 339 339 test motions are encoded by
the same ASL3DWord MoAE used elsewhere; pairwise L 2 distances in the latent are partitioned into same-gloss pairs
( 874 874 pairs, both encodings GT clips of the same target gloss) and different-gloss pairs ( 113,708 113{,}708 ). The same-gloss mean
distance ( 0.826 0.826 ) divided by the different-gloss mean distance
( 1.098 1.098 ) gives ρ faith , ref = 0.752 \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752 , the lowest ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} achievable
on this MoAE under perfect within-class generation. The checkpoint’s 0.73 0.73 is 0.022 0.022 below this value, meaning generated motion is, in the
MoAE latent, on average as close to its target as a second GT clip of
the same gloss. Consequently the gap between ASL3DWord ( 0.73 0.73 ) and the
How2Sign band ( [ 0.89 , 1.00 ] [0.89,1.00] ) understates the actual difference:
How2Sign checkpoints sit 0.04 0.04 – 0.15 0.15 above their 0.849 0.849 reference,

band [ 0.89 , 1.00 ] [0.89,1.00] regardless of which combination is used. Backbones (2). Standard : the MDM denoiser of Fig. S2 a. Multi-scale temporal transformer ( MSTrans ) : the
same denoiser with the encoder replaced by a 4 4 -scale temporal encoder at frame-rate factors 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 1,2,4,8 with
cross-scale fusion, intended to capture multi-rate motion structure
(slow trajectory + + fast hand articulation): the noisy motion is
processed at strides 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 1,2,4,8 by four independent Transformer
encoders, each cross-attending to the text token, and the per-scale
features are upsampled to T T frames and fused. It changes FID by < 0.2 <0.2 and ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} by ≤ 0.02 \leq 0.02 ( Tab. S1 , rows 3–4). Conditioning inputs. Raw sentence , encoded
by the frozen text encoder and pooled to a single token; LLM
keywords ( Sec. B ); on the gloss-annotated corpora also native gloss and the fused string. The text encoder is
CLIP-ViT-B/32 [ 17 ] for English and German and the
Chinese-CLIP text tower [ 25 ] for Chinese, using
its CLS token after the contrastive projection (mean-pooled hidden
states form a new anisotropic cone and are not used). On How2Sign we
additionally tested a phonology-augmented keyword input with
per-token phonological-attribute embeddings
following Hong and Kosecka [9] ; its collapse pattern is
unchanged and it is not separately tabulated. Loss and sampling. Per-frame pose MSE plus an FK
joint-position MSE term. All MDM variants are trained with
classifier-free guidance ( 10 % 10\% condition dropout) and sampled with
guidance scale 3.0 3.0 ; the Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily runs use T = 100 T=100 , batch size 64 64 , and 100 100 epochs, identical across the
sentence, keyword, gloss, and fused variants of a corpus. Clean regression model. The clean regression model is a 6 6 -layer Transformer
decoder [ 23 ] with D = 512 D=512 , 8 8 heads, 0.1 0.1 dropout, GELU. The decoder’s queries are T T learnable positional
embeddings; cross-attention memory is a single text token from the
frozen text encoder. The output projects to 132 132 upper-body axis-angle dimensions. Training: AdamW
( β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} ), OneCycleLR schedule with 5 % 5\% warmup and cosine annealing,
fp16 mixed precision. Loss is ℒ pose + λ FK ​ ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} (per-frame pose MSE and FK joint-position MSE) with λ FK = 5 \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=5 . Total trainable parameters ∼ \sim 26 26 M
(with frozen text encoder excluded). Phoenix-2014T and CSL-Daily
regression runs use batch size 64 64 , lr 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and 100 100 / 65 65 epochs respectively (the CSL-Daily evaluation loss plateaus from
epoch ∼ \sim 70 70 ; the reported checkpoint is the best-validation one). Differences from Progressive Transformers (PT). The clean regression model differs from
PT [ 19 ] in four ways:
(i) we generate all T T frames in a single forward pass, whereas PT
is autoregressive (one frame at a time);
(ii) output length T T is fixed per sample, whereas PT uses a
learned step counter to decide when to stop, which the released
protocol drives with GT timing at inference ( Sec. H );
(iii) the text encoder is frozen CLIP (a single pooled
token), whereas PT trains its own text encoder over T5-style
tokenization;
(iv) the decoder sees only the text embedding via cross-attention,
with no feedback from previously generated frames.
These simplifications remove any dependence on GT timing at
inference and let the row report what a basic Transformer-decoder + + text cross-attention recipe achieves
at the same paired-data budget. Vocabulary-restricted training subsets. The K = 3000 K{=}3000 and K = 500 K{=}500 whitelists, as well as the ≤ 1 \leq 1 -word
and ≤ 3 \leq 3 -word short-sentence whitelists, are derived from
frequencies on How2Sign train. The K = K K{=}K filter keeps only
sentences whose words are all within the top- K K most-frequent
training-vocabulary words. The whitelist is always defined on
the raw-sentence vocabulary regardless of whether the model receives
the sentence or the LLM keywords as input; the sent and keywords variants in Tab. S1 therefore share the
same set of training and test sentences and differ only in the
conditioning modality. For each variant we store the train and test
sentence lists under the same train-frequency vocab, ensuring
within-distribution evaluation. Counts (train / test): K = 3000 K{=}3000 : 13,571 / 890 13{,}571/890 ; K = 500 K{=}500 : 2,918 / 241 2{,}918/241 ; ≤ 3 \leq 3 -word: 1,502 / 121 1{,}502/121 ; ≤ 1 \leq 1 -word: 564 / 44 564/44 . E Per-dataset GT-vs-GT reference protocol Eq. (9) defines ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} as the mean latent distance
between two GT renditions of the same text divided by the mean latent
distance between renditions of different texts. All references use the
dataset’s own frozen MoAE, the same root-zeroing and T = 100 T=100 resampling as the diagnostic, and pairs drawn exactly as for the
generator (numerator and denominator on the same rendition pool).
Table 1 lists the group and pair counts; the mean
latent distances (same-text / different-text pairs) behind each value
are ASL3DWord 0.826 / 1.098 0.826/1.098 , Phoenix-2014T 2.167 / 2.479 2.167/2.479 , CSL-Daily 1.236 / 1.836 1.236/1.836 , How2Sign 3.346 / 3.940 3.346/3.940 (all cross-video repeats: 5.230 / 5.248 5.230/5.248 ). ASL3DWord. Groups are glosses; 100 100 of the 103 103 test
glosses have ≥ 2 \geq 2 clips (different signers). Same-gloss pairs are
across signers by construction. Phoenix-2014T. Groups are exact German sentences recurring
with ≥ 2 \geq 2 renditions in the pooled train + + test split (dev
excluded); 50 50 such sentences exist, mostly formulaic broadcast
openers and closers. Many renditions share a signer, which makes the
reference conservative (same-signer pairs are closer than cross-signer
pairs, lowering ρ faith , ref \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}} and making it harder to reach). CSL-Daily. Every training sentence is re-performed by
several signers ( 2.8 2.8 on average, up to 6 6 ), so same-text groups are
abundant ( ∼ \sim 6.5 6.5 K); we sample 1,000 1{,}000 groups (seed fixed) from
the pooled train + + test split, dev excluded. 99.6 % 99.6\% of same-sentence
pairs are cross-signer (only 9 9 of 2,504 2{,}504 share a signer): the CSL
reference measures scripted cross-signer consistency, the strictest of
the four. How2Sign. Pooled train + + test contains 789 789 exact-repeat
groups ( 2,338 2{,}338 renditions), but most are within-video: re-alignment
overlaps, duplicated metadata rows, or same-take repeats (e.g. exercise counting), which carry no independent rendition. Restricting
to repeats across distinct videos leaves 181 181 groups
( 923 923 renditions), dominated by one- and two-word greetings and
fillers (“Hi!”, “Okay?”, “Cheers!”) whose clips carry no
sentence-specific motion: same-text pairs are as far apart as random
pairs and the reference reads 0.997 0.997 , i.e. the metric correctly
reporting a signal-free condition. We therefore report the reference on
the 50 50 sentences of ≥ 5 \geq 5 words recurring across distinct videos
( 116 116 renditions; typically intro/outro scripts re-performed across a
signer’s video series), which gives 0.849 0.849 , consistent with the
Phoenix and ASL3DWord values. Both numbers are disclosed; all 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints ( 0.89 0.89 – 1.00 1.00 ) lie above the 0.849 0.849 reference. F Coverage analyses and controls Conditioning-space dispersion. Two measures per corpus, computed on the same frozen text encoder the

the last row re-measures CSL-Daily on the Chinese-CLIP text tower
that the reported CSL-Daily models condition on):

pairwise cosine among training-sentence embeddings (subsample of 4,000 4{,}000 sentences, ∼ \sim 8 8 M pairs); (b) coverage , each
test sentence’s cosine to its nearest training neighbor (full pool).

(train centroid subtracted and renormalized, which removes the

motion as the “prediction”, encode it with the dataset’s MoAE, and

indistinguishable from the random-pairing null at every quantile, so
no subpopulation of test sentences finds a matching training motion.

but compared per frame : the frame distance is the L 2 distance between the two 44 × 3 44\times 3 joint sets, and the
alignment cost is the mean frame distance along the optimal
dynamic-time-warping path. We report the ratio of this cost for the
generation and its own GT to the cost for the generation and the GT of
an unrelated sentence ( DTW/random ; 1 1 = chance). The equal-timestamp variant uses the diagonal path instead of the
DTW path ( diag/random ). The human–human baseline applies the
identical statistic to two GT renditions of the same sentence ( 40 40 same-text groups per corpus, pooled train + + test); the generation
statistic uses 40 40 test sentences (seed 42 42 ; unseen sentences for
CSL-Daily), a sample disjoint from the four rendered sentences per
corpus. Table S6 : Frame-level alignability (lower = more alignable). DTW/random
statistics over 40 40 pairs each; the last column is the equal-timestamp
(no DTW) mean. (i) Two humans are far from frame-identical ( 0.74 0.74 on Phoenix-2014T, 0.59 0.59 on CSL-Daily), so a single GT video demands more consistency
than signers exhibit. (ii) Generation sits one band above the human
distribution on both corpora; normalized to each corpus’s own human
mean, Phoenix-2014T stands at 1.16 × 1.16\times and CSL-Daily at 1.29 × 1.29\times , the same ordering as the sequence-level MoAE verdicts.

reaches the human mean, and it is populated by the densest conditions:

error: the equal-timestamp ratio is 0.98 0.98 / 0.97 0.97 for generations and
inflates even the human–human pairs to 0.92 0.92 / 0.78 0.78 . GT-timeline
frame strips therefore overstate mismatch, and all figures show
