bottom), complementing Fig. 3. (a) articulated,
sentence-dependent signing whose trajectory does not follow this GT
rendition; (b) an unseen CSL-Daily sentence at the generation median. H Code-level audit of Progressive Transformers A prominent Phoenix SLP system, Progressive
Transformers [ 19 ] , reports better BLEU
than our checkpoints. Reading the released code, we find three
inference/evaluation paths that leak ground-truth timing or length
into the reported protocol; the two most important are (L1) the
predicted counter scalar is overwritten by the GT counter at every
decoder step, and (L2) the inference output length is set to the GT
sequence length rather than learned via a stop signal. PT on the clean Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X data (Sec. 6.5). We retrained the official PT code on the same SOKE SMPL-X Phoenix data
as our MDM and regression models (FK-lifted to the 44 44 -joint 3 3 D
space the MoAE consumes) and ran inference twice on the same
checkpoint. Under fair inference (counter and length governed by the
model’s own predictions) PT collapses: ρ faith = 0.9999 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9999 , ρ div = 0.025 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.025 , d inter = 0.08 d_{\rm inter}=0.08 against a GT spread of 3.26 3.26 .
Under the paper’s leaky protocol (GT counter and length supplied at
inference) ρ faith = 0.9974 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.9974 and ρ div = 0.223 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}=0.223 : the leak inflates
apparent output diversity ∼ \sim 9 × 9\times while leaving faithfulness at
chance. MDM ( 0.839 0.839 ) and the clean regression model ( 0.811 0.811 ) are
faithful on the identical data. The remainder of this section reports
the earlier leaky-vs-fair experiment on PT’s own pose representation,
which reaches the same conclusion. Leaky-vs-fair experiment. We retrained PT’s released code on Phoenix-2014T at the paper’s native
data scale and “best T2P” configuration, with no changes to
architecture, loss, training, or inference logic, then ran inference
twice on the same checkpoint over all 632 632 test sentences:
once with leaks (L1)+(L2) intact (“leaky”), once with all three
leaks off (“fair”, counter and length governed purely by the
model’s predictions). Outputs were encoded with the Phoenix MediaPipe
MoAE ( Sec. D ) and d inter d_{\rm inter} / ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} / ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} computed on the full test split ( Tab. S7 ). Representation and extraction. The independent PT retrainings cited in the main text use
OpenPose-derived 3D joints [ 10 , 24 ] or a
SMPL-X representation [ 26 ] , and PT’s original
pipeline uses OpenPose. For this experiment we extract Phoenix poses
with MediaPipe Holistic, because OpenPose’s released codebase has very
limited maintenance and is difficult to deploy in a modern
environment. This extraction is imperfect: across the Phoenix train
split, 28.6 % 28.6\% of left-hand and 23.9 % 23.9\% of right-hand frames are
returned with no detection and are interpolated (see hand-detection
notes below). We therefore use the leaky-vs-fair result only as a within-checkpoint comparison (the checkpoint, and any
extraction artefact, is held fixed across the two inference passes,
so the contrast still isolates the leak), and do not report absolute
PT performance from this retraining; the SMPL-X retraining above
uses the same clean data as every other Phoenix model in the paper. Table S7: Toggling PT’s inference-time GT-timing/length leak on a single retrained checkpoint (MediaPipe representation). d inter d_{\rm inter} is the mean pairwise L2 distance between generated
samples in the MoAE latent; ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} normalises it by the GT spread.
The checkpoint is held fixed, so the comparison isolates the leak’s
effect. Metric Fair (no leak) Leaky (paper) d inter d_{\rm inter} 0.031 0.031 0.207 0.207 d inter ​ - ​ GT d_{\rm inter\text{-}GT} 2.321 2.321 2.321 2.321 ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} (inter / GT) 0.013 0.089 ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} 0.999 0.999 0.996 0.996 Findings. (i) The leak measurably changes PT’s output. Toggling the
GT-timing/length leak on the same trained checkpoint inflates the
inter-sample spread d inter d_{\rm inter} from 0.031 0.031 to 0.207 0.207 and the
diversity ratio ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} from 0.013 0.013 to 0.089 0.089 , a roughly
sevenfold change ( Tab. S7 ), while ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} stays at
chance ( 0.999 → 0.996 0.999\to 0.996 ). Because the checkpoint is held fixed
across the two inference passes, this isolates the leak: the
GT-aligned timing it supplies materially affects the generated motion
and any statistic computed from it, without making the motion any
more faithful to its sentence.
(ii) Fair inference does not learn end-of-sequence in our
text-to-pose setting. Without the GT counter, the predicted counter
never crosses the stop threshold: every one of the 632 632 test
samples runs to the 300 300 -frame cap, while GT lengths range from 3 3 to 89 89 frames. Under text conditioning, PT’s continuous-output
decoder relies on (L1) for inference-time length supervision; a
gloss-conditioned PT, whose input already encodes sign count, retains
a partial length signal (leak-free gloss-to-pose PT reaches BLEU-4 4.04 4.04 ; 10 ). The rest of this section gives the full L1–L3 enumeration, the
training setup for the leaky-vs-fair experiment, and the supporting
pose-extractor, hand-detection, and bug-fix notes needed to make the
released code execute under modern tooling. Three inference- and evaluation-time leaks. Inspection of the released repository identifies the following three
paths through which GT timing or length information enters PT’s
reported numerical protocol: (L1) search.py :55–63: at every decoder step the
predicted counter scalar c ^ t \hat{c}_{t} is overwritten with the GT
counter c t ∗ c^{*}_{t} before being fed back. The author comment in the file
reads: “ Drive the timing by giving the GT timing ”. (L2) search.py :46: the inference output length is
assigned from the GT target length rather than learned via a stop
signal. (L3) Configs/Base.yaml :25,29: the only
validation/early-stopping metric is the DTW score itself, so the
reported quantitative results come from this GT-aligned distance. Training setup and toggle list. Training matched the paper’s data scale ( ∼ \sim 7 000 7\,000 training
sequences) and the published “best T2P” configuration ( 2 2 encoder/decoder layers, 4 4 heads, 512 512 embedding dim, MSE loss,
future-prediction FP = 10 \mathrm{FP}{=}10 , Gaussian-noise augmentation rate 5 5 ). Training reached lr min \mathrm{lr}_{\min} at step 1450 1450 , with best
validation DTW = 15.76 =15.76 at step 450 450 . The “leaky” inference
configuration in Tab. S7 leaves (L1)+(L2) intact
(matching the paper’s reported protocol up to BLEU back-translation);
the “fair” configuration disables all three leaks listed above
(counter is purely autoregressive, output length is governed by a
predicted-counter stop rule capped at the global 300 300 -frame limit,
and the DTW-aligned distance is no longer used as the
model-selection metric). Both inference passes were run over all 632 632 test sentences on the same trained checkpoint. Pose extraction divergence from the original paper. Saunders et al. [ 19 ] use OpenPose
followed by 2D-to-3D inverse-kinematics lifting; we substitute
MediaPipe Holistic upper-body keypoints because the OpenPose pipeline
is impractical to re-deploy on contemporary GPU toolchains and the
extraction is not released. The two extractors differ in keypoint set
and 2D-vs-3D representation, but the total paired-sample budget is
identical at ∼ \sim 7 000 7\,000 training sequences, so the
leak audit still applies; what we cannot precisely
reproduce are the absolute pose-space FID values (which depend on
extraction). Hand-detection failure rate. MediaPipe Holistic produces all-zero hand keypoints when detection
confidence is below threshold. Across the Phoenix train split, the
mean per-video fraction of fully-missing left-hand frames is 28.6 % 28.6\% (max 100 % 100\% ); for the right hand 23.9 % 23.9\% (max 84 % 84\% ). We
linearly-interpolate within each clip and fall back to the corresponding
body wrist when an entire hand is missing throughout, so PT does not
train against zero-hand targets. Bug fixes required to run the released code under a
modern deep-learning toolchain. We applied six small patches to make
the released code execute under the current toolchain. None of
the patches touch the architecture, loss, training loop, validation
loss/DTW computation, model selection, or inference/search code : the
model and training-relevant files ( model.py , transformer_layers.py , encoders.py , decoders.py , embeddings.py , loss.py , search.py , data.py , batch.py , vocabulary.py ) are byte-for-byte the released versions.
The patches are: removing the deprecated verbose kwarg from ReduceLROnPlateau ( builders.py:137 ); fixing an
undefined train_output reference ( prediction.py:73 );
removing a redundant FP-cut on the inference output already cut in search.py:greedy ( prediction.py:74 ); making plot_videos.py:47 adaptive to MediaPipe’s 67 67 -joint layout;
wrapping produce_validation_video in try/except to swallow
bone-graph mismatches at validation-video render time (the _save_checkpoint call lies outside the try block, so model
selection is unaffected); and adding weights_only=False to torch.load ( helpers.py:202 ). Total diff vs the
upstream repo: 32 32 lines added, 20 20 lines removed across 5 5 files. Reproducibility. The patched code, training and audit scripts, configurations, and all
per-sample inference outputs are available alongside the paper.
Reproducing Tab. S7 end-to-end requires only a single
GPU.
